opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. For me, the problems that matter most usually sit right at the boundary between what people want to do with machine learning and what the current systems actually let them do. I've always found that the most interesting work comes from feeling that friction yourself.

When I was working on XGBoost, it wasn't because I set out to build a famous library. I was a student doing machine learning research, and I kept running into the fact that the tools were too slow or didn't scale to the data I cared about. So the question became: what if we really took the systems side seriously? Things like memory layout, cache awareness, and distributed computation. That turned out to unlock a lot for many people, not just me.

TVM came from a similar place. Deep learning was exploding, and there were many models and many kinds of hardware: GPUs, mobile chips, specialized accelerators. But every combination required a lot of hand engineering. To me, that gap was a signal. If every new model or chip needs a team of experts to make it run well, that's a systems problem that deserves a more general, automated solution. That's where machine learning compilation came in.

So a few principles guide me. First, look for problems where you're the user, or very close to the users, because then you understand what actually hurts. Second, ask whether solving it would enable other people to do things they couldn't do before. In ML systems, the impact often comes from lowering the barrier so that more people can build, deploy, and experiment. Third, try to find the abstraction underneath the immediate pain. A one-off optimization is useful, but the bigger win is identifying the right layer, the right interface, so that the solution generalizes as models and hardware keep changing.

And honestly, I also think it's important to build things and put them out in the open. Open source has been a huge part of how I learn which problems matter. When people start using your system in ways you never expected, they tell you very quickly what's important and what's not. That feedback loop between research and real-world usage is, I think, one of the most valuable things in this field.

Right now, with large language models, I see the same pattern again. Everyone wants to run these models everywhere, on servers, on laptops, on phones, in the browser. Making that possible efficiently and universally is, to me, one of the most exciting problems at the moment.

r001.rationale: The response says research problems emerge from current practical friction, such as systems failing to meet users’ needs as machine learning and its uses evolve.

r002.rationale: It identifies the diversity of hardware and the hand engineering needed for each model and chip combination as a bottleneck motivating machine-learning compilation.

r003.rationale: The response mentions hand engineering to make model and chip combinations run well, but does not clearly identify software bring-up itself as a bottleneck.

r004.rationale: The response advocates a general, automated compilation solution, but does not raise using AI to optimize machine-learning systems engineering as a research question.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say the way I think about it has changed over the years, but one principle has stayed fairly constant: I try to pick problems where there's a real gap between what people want to do and what the current tools let them do, and where closing that gap is going to be useful to a lot of people, not just to one paper.

When I worked on XGBoost, for example, the motivation was very concrete. People were running gradient boosting in competitions and in industry, and the existing implementations were either slow or didn't scale, or they were hard to use in practice. It wasn't a problem that looked glamorous from a pure research point of view, but the moment you make something ten or a hundred times faster and make it actually robust, suddenly a whole community can do things they couldn't do before. So one signal I look for is: if this works, does it change what practitioners can realistically attempt?

The second thing I pay attention to is where the hardware and the models are going, and where the software stack is going to crack. Machine learning systems sit in between an exploding space of models on one side and an exploding space of hardware on the other. Every time there's a new kind of model, or a new accelerator, or a new deployment target like a phone or a browser, there's a huge amount of engineering that has to be redone, and that's usually a sign that there's an abstraction missing. That was really the motivation behind TVM and later the MLC work. Instead of hand-writing kernels for every combination, can we build a compiler and a representation so that this effort becomes automatic, or at least much cheaper? So I'm always asking: what's the repeated, painful work that lots of people are doing by hand, and can we turn it into a system?

The third thing, honestly, is timing. A lot of good problems are good problems five years too early or five years too late. You want to pick something where the demand is just starting to become visible, so that by the time you build it out, people actually need it. Large language models running on local devices is a good example. A few years ago it would have looked like an odd thing to spend time on. Now it's obviously important, and the systems questions around memory, quantization, and portability are very real.

And then the last thing I'd say is that I like problems where building the thing is itself the research. In ML systems, you often don't fully understand the problem until you've built a version of the solution and watched it fail. So I tend to favor problems where we can get something working end to end, put it in people's hands, and let the feedback tell us what the actual hard questions are. The open-source community has been incredibly important for that. It turns what could be an isolated academic exercise into something that's continuously being tested against reality, and that's really how I figure out which parts matter.

r001.rationale: The response prioritizes problems based on practical gaps, broad usefulness, and when demand is emerging, tying research priorities to the needs of machine learning at a given time.

r002.rationale: It says new accelerators require substantial engineering to adapt software and describes this as a sign of a missing abstraction motivating TVM and later work.

r003.rationale: It identifies repeated manual work—rewriting kernels across models, hardware, and deployment targets—as painful engineering that compilation can automate or reduce.

r004.rationale: The response asks whether a compiler and representation can automate systems work, but it does not raise using AI to optimize machine-learning systems engineering.

astra-6.text:
I think a good starting point is to ask what is preventing people from doing something they want to do. Is it the cost of training? Is it the difficulty of deploying a model on a particular device? Is it that trying a new idea requires rewriting a large amount of software? Those barriers give us concrete problems to work on.

Then the research question is: is there a more general idea behind that particular problem? You can optimize one workload, and that can be useful. But if you find an abstraction that helps many workloads, or lets other people explore ideas more easily, the impact can be much larger.

So I would look for both a real need and an opportunity to generalize. And I think you have to keep testing your assumptions by building things and seeing how people use them. Sometimes the bottleneck you thought was important turns out to be less important than something you overlooked.

r001.rationale: It says research should start from practical barriers to what people want to do, and that the most important bottleneck can change as assumptions are tested.

r002.rationale: It mentions difficulty deploying models on a particular device, but does not identify hardware adaptation as a reason to continue machine-learning compilation research.

r003.rationale: It cites rewriting software as a practical barrier, but does not connect software bring-up to continued machine-learning compilation research.

r004.rationale: It does not raise using AI to optimize machine-learning systems engineering as a research question.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a useful starting point is to ask: what is preventing people from doing something they want to do? In machine-learning systems, that might be the cost of running a model, the difficulty of deploying it, or the amount of effort needed to try a new idea. Then the research question is whether we can remove that barrier in a way that helps more than one particular application.

There’s a balance between solving a concrete problem and finding the right abstraction. If you stay too specific, you might build something that works once. If you start too abstract, you might solve a problem that nobody has. I like the process of building something, seeing where it breaks, and using that experience to refine the research question.

Ultimately, I would ask: if we succeed, what becomes possible, and who can benefit from it? That helps connect an interesting technical problem to something that matters.

r001.rationale: The response says research can start from practical barriers, but does not explain that priorities arise from the major problems facing machine learning at a given time.

r002.rationale: It mentions model cost and deployment difficulty, but does not identify adapting to hardware as a bottleneck in machine-learning compilation.

r003.rationale: It mentions deployment difficulty generally, but does not identify software bring-up as a bottleneck in machine-learning compilation.

r004.rationale: The response does not raise using AI to optimize machine-learning systems engineering as a research question.
